The Book states the pairing in verse after verse, as when it says that God is the one who gives life and causes death (53:44 — *“And He is the One Who gives life and causes death”*), when it describes him as the one who gives life and causes death and who only has to say "Be!" for a matter to exist (40:68 — *“He is the One Who gives life and causes death. When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is”*). When it says that he created death and life as a test of who would act best (67:2 — *“˹He is the One˺ Who created death and life in order to test which of you is best in deeds. And He is the Almighty, All-Forgiving”*). The denial of the resurrection begins with a misreading of the most ordinary fact available: that a person did not give himself life and cannot keep it.

**The Gathering After the Dying**

The third clause of the sentence moves past the point at which the deniers stopped. After life and death comes the gathering on the Day of Judgment, and the Book attaches the same certainty to it in other places: God has taken it upon himself to be merciful, and he will certainly gather all of humanity together on that Day about which there is no doubt (6:12 — *“He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt.”*). The order of the three clauses is the order of the argument. The first two are uncontested facts that the deniers themselves had admitted in different words; the third follows from the nature of the one who performs the first two. If a person's life is given and taken by a power outside himself, the question of what happens to him afterwards is not settled by the observation that his body lies in the ground.

**"But Most People Do Not Know"**

The clause appears throughout the Book in nearly the same wording. It serves as a frame for a certain kind of fact: people do not know about the Hour (7:187 — *“Say, “That knowledge is only with Allah, but most people do not know.”*), most people do not know that the Prophet was sent to all of humanity (34:28 — *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a deliverer of good news and a warner to all of humanity, but most people do not know”*), and most do not know that God gives life and death. The repetition is not contempt for the human race; it is an accurate description of a majority condition on matters of the unseen, and the Book uses it to prepare the believer for being in the minority. The sentence is delivered to an audience that had just made a demand, and the clause tells them, in plain language, what their position amounts to. They are not the holders of a difficult truth. They are the people who do not know.
verses.27:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. On the Day the Hour will be established, the people of falsehood will then be in ˹total˺ loss

**Authority Stated as Ownership**

The verse opens with a claim of ownership, and the Book states it again and again in almost the same words: to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. He is capable of everything (3:189 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Most Capable of everything”*); to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them (5:17 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between.”*). To him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and to him is the return (24:42 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. And to Allah is the final return”*); and to him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, forgiving whom he wills and punishing whom he wills (48:14 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). The repetition is not padding. It is the foundation on which every other claim in the chapter rests, because a court that will judge all things must first own all things. No part of the sky or the ground lies outside the jurisdiction that the verse announces, and the denial of that kingdom is the mistake that all the sūrah's opponents have in common.

**Loss Described in the Book's Own Vocabulary**

The Book has a whole vocabulary for losing, and it uses it in the commercial register the sūrah's readers knew well. Elsewhere it says that those who have ruined themselves will never believe (6:12 — *“But those who have ruined themselves will never believe”*); that those who have lost their souls will never believe (6:20 — *“Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him ˹to be a true prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Those who have ruined themselves will never believe”*); that on the Day the warning is fulfilled the wrongdoers will say that the messengers brought the truth. Will ask for intercessors and for a return, only to find that they have lost themselves and that what they fabricated has failed them (7:53 — *“They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”*; 11:21 — *“It is they who have ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”*); that those whose scales are light have doomed themselves (23:103 — *“But those whose scale is light, they will have doomed themselves, staying in Hell forever”*); and that the true losers are those who lose themselves and their families on the Day of Judgment, which the Book calls the clearest loss (39:15 — *“Say, “The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day.”*; 42:45 — *“And the believers will say, “The ˹true˺ losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on Judgment Day.”*). The vocabulary is consistent because the concept is: a person has one capital, and losing it cannot be reversed.

**A Loss Measured by What Was Fabricated**

Another chapter states the outcome in a way that completes this verse: they have ruined themselves, and whatever gods they fabricated will fail them (11:21 — *“It is they who have ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”*). What a person builds against the truth is exactly what he loses, and the sūrah has already named a man who took his own desires as a god. That project has an end, and the verse before us announces it. The loss is not an arbitrary penalty imposed from outside; it is the collapse of the structure that was raised in place of the truth, and its collapse takes its builder with it. The Book's language of trade returns here at full strength: what the people of falsehood invested in is worthless, and the Day will be the moment the market finds out.
verses.28:
> And you will see every faith-community on its knees. Every community will be summoned to its record ˹of deeds˺. ˹They all will be told,˺ “This Day you will be rewarded for what you used to do

**A Scene Nobody Can Stand Above**

The verse puts the whole of humanity in one posture. Every community appears on its knees, and the word translated community covers religious bodies and nations, the groups into which people have divided themselves across history. The sūrah takes its name from this scene, and the image has the effect of cancelling every distinction the earlier verses have been examining — the allies who protected one another, the leaders who held their ground, the scholars who disputed, the men who followed their appetites. All of them are kneeling. The Book elsewhere pictures a different moment in which people arrive with heads raised and eyes fixed, unable to blink, their hearts empty (14:43 — *“rushing forth, heads raised, never blinking, hearts void”*), and the two images belong to the same day. What the verse does with a single word is to show that the audience of the judgment is comprehensive.

**Summoned to Its Record**

The verse moves from the posture to the procedure. Each community is called to its book, and the Book elsewhere describes the same scene with the record laid open, the guilty afraid of what is written in it, crying out that nothing, small or great, has been left out, and finding everything they did present before them (18:49 — *“They will find whatever they did present ˹before them˺.”*). The records are mentioned in several places: an angel is said to record every soul (86:4 — *“There is no soul without a vigilant angel ˹recording everything˺”*). The books are kept by honoured scribes who know what people do (82:10–12 — *“honourable angels, recording ˹everything˺”*). A person is bound to his destiny and will be handed a record that he finds spread open (17:13 — *“We have bound every human’s destiny to their neck. And on the Day of Judgment We will bring forth to each ˹person˺ a record which they will find laid open”*); and the command is given to him to read his own book, since he is enough that day to reckon with himself (17:14 — *“˹And it will be said,˺ “Read your record. You ˹alone˺ are sufficient this Day to take account of yourself.”*). The image is forensic, and it is built on documents rather than on testimony.

**One Ledger, or One Book for All?**

Commentators differ about whether the singular "book" names a single register or the collection of each person's individual ledger. Some take it as the record kept for each individual by the angels at God's command, gathered for the occasion so that the community appears with all its files at once. Others take it as the Preserved Tablet, the register in which everything has been inscribed and which is described in another chapter as a well-guarded writing (85:22 — *“˹recorded˺ in a Preserved Tablet”*). The first reading explains why a community can be told to appear with its book, since the books of its members would be brought together; the second explains the singular and the thoroughness of the record. The difference does not affect the doctrine, which is that nothing has been lost, and it does not affect the verse's drama, which is that the file being read is your own.

**"This Day You Will Be Rewarded for What You Used to Do"**

The address is direct and it names the standard of payment: what you used to do, in the habitual sense the imperfect tense carries. People will not be judged for their final moments or for a single gesture made under pressure; the criterion is the pattern of a life. The Book states the same rule elsewhere, saying that no soul will be wronged in the least and that people will be rewarded only for what they used to do (36:54 — *“On that Day no soul will be wronged in the least, nor will you be rewarded except for what you used to do”*). The wording also closes an exit. A person cannot plead the difficulty of his circumstances, since the circumstances were part of what he used to do, nor can he plead that his intentions were good while the pattern was something else. The sentence read out on that day is drawn from the ordinary texture of a lifetime.
verses.29:
> This record of Ours speaks the truth about you. Indeed, We always had your deeds recorded ˹by the angels˺.”

**The Book That Speaks**

The record is not described as evidence waiting to be interpreted but as a speaker. It gives testimony, and what it says about the people standing in front of it is true in a way that cannot be corrected or softened. The Book's phrase for accuracy is repeated in several places where the outcome of a matter is announced, and the point of the metaphor is the absence of any party through whom the truth could be bent. Other passages picture the same document being handed over and read: the record is laid open and the wicked see what is in it and cry out at its completeness (18:49 — *“And the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, and you will see the wicked in fear of what is ˹written˺ in it.”*).

**What "Our Book" Claims**

The possessive is doing real work. The record belongs to God, and the scribes who filled it were acting under his command rather than in pursuit of their own interests. The Book describes them elsewhere: every soul has a vigilant angel recording what it does (86:4 — *“There is no soul without a vigilant angel ˹recording everything˺”*). The scribes are honoured and they know whatever people do (82:11–12 — *“They know whatever you do”*); and two recording angels sit to the right and the left of each person, so that no word is uttered without an observer ready to write it down (50:17–18 — *“not a word does a person utter without having a ˹vigilant˺ observer ready ˹to write it down˺”*). The picture removes another possible objection, which is that the record might reflect the bias of its authors. Nothing in the account suggests that the angels interpret or evaluate what they write. They note, and the noting belongs to a system whose owner is the judge.

**The Book as a Proof For or Against Its Reader**

The Prophet's teaching supplies the frame for this scene in a single sentence preserved in the most authoritative collections. Abu Malik al-Ashʿarī narrates that the Messenger of God said, among a series of images for the parts of faith, that the Qur'an is a proof for you or against you (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 223). The report captures exactly what this verse is describing. The recitation that was delivered in this world will function at the judgment as evidence, and whether it is evidence for the reader or against him depends on what he did when it reached him. The sūrah has shown both cases: those who mocked the verses and those who received them with certainty, and the same words belong to the file of both.

**Truth That Cannot Be Edited**

The phrase rendered "with truth" marks the record as incapable of error in either direction. It does not exaggerate a good deed, and it does not omit a sin. The Book makes the same guarantee about the scenes of judgment in several places, and it states elsewhere that not the smallest atom's weight of good or evil will be missing from the accounting (99:7–8 — *“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it”*). The certainty that this removes is a comfort to the wronged: nothing they suffered has been forgotten, and nothing their oppressors did has been mislaid. It is a warning to the wrongdoer for the same reason: no favourable circumstance of the trial has been overlooked. The record is complete, and the chapter's argument throughout has been that completeness is what the deniers were really hoping to avoid.
verses.30:
> As for those who believed and did good, their Lord will admit them into His mercy. That is ˹truly˺ the absolute triumph

**Two Conditions, Never Separated**

The Qur'an almost never mentions faith without attaching action to it, and this verse belongs to that pattern. The phrase describes people who believed and did good, and the two verbs are joined so closely that they read as a single description of one life. The Book does the same thing in dozens of places, and the practice is consistent enough to be treated as a rule: belief is the root, and good deeds are the fruit that shows the root is alive. What the verse does not do is split the pair, so that a reader who claims faith while his conduct ignores it has no verse to lean on. Nor does it accept a life of good works with no belief behind them, since a deed is given its value by the one to whom the doer is answering.

**The Absolute Triumph**

The word translated here names the winning of a contest or the achieving of a goal, and the Book uses it for the final success of those whose business in this world ended in profit. It is not a modest reward; it is the great achievement, and the Book reserves the phrase for the states that no loss can reach, since everything earned in this world can be taken away. The same expression appears in the scene where the faithful are told that God is pleased with them and they with him, and that this is the greatest triumph (5:119 — *“Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.”*). A farmer who brings in a harvest, a merchant who closes a profitable voyage, and a traveller who arrives at his destination are all pictures the Book draws on. The verse's chosen phrase is the last of them: arrival after a journey, in a place where no further journey begins.
verses.31:
> And as for those who disbelieved, ˹they will be told,˺ “Were My revelations not recited to you, yet you acted arrogantly and were a wicked people

**A Question Put to the Condemned**

The address at the judgment is a question, and the form is important. The disbelievers are not lectured about their crimes; they are asked whether something happened, and the answer is already known to everyone present. The Book uses this construction at the reckoning in several places, and it has a double edge. It forces the accused to acknowledge the fact under discussion, and it removes any possibility of complaint about a verdict delivered without notice. The sentence also shows who is speaking. The voice says "My revelations" — the first person singular, the voice of God at the hearing — so the question is not put by an angel reading a charge sheet. The owner of the message is asking the men who rejected it whether it reached them.

**"Were Not My Revelations Recited to You?"**

The question names the central fact of the case. The message was delivered, in their language, in their city, by a man they knew. The Book records elsewhere that the same admission is drawn from the people of the Fire when the keepers of Hell ask them whether messengers did not come to them reciting the revelations of their Lord and warning them about the meeting with that Day (39:71 — *“When they arrive there, its gates will be opened and its keepers will ask them: “Did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, reciting to you the revelations of your Lord and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?”*). The answer in that scene is yes, and the keepers reply to their plea for prayer by asking whether messengers did not come with clear proofs, to which they again answer yes (40:50 — *“The keepers will reply, “Did your messengers not ˹constantly˺ come to you with clear proofs?”*). The pattern in the Book is consistent: the condemned never claim that they were left uninformed. What they lose at the judgment is not an argument but a hope, and the question in this verse is the first movement of that loss.
verses.32:
> And whenever it was said ˹to you˺, ‘Surely Allah’s promise ˹of judgment˺ is true and there is no doubt about the Hour,’ you said ˹mockingly˺, ‘We do not know what the Hour is! We think it is no more than speculation, and we are not convinced ˹that it will ever come˺.’”

**The Reply Recorded Word for Word**

The verse continues the judgment address and quotes the defendants directly. This is the Book's characteristic method of reporting an argument: the opponents' case is given in their own terms, without caricature, before it is answered. Here the words are spoken at the reckoning, so their content has a second function, since it now serves as testimony against the people who said it. The sentence is short and its components are ordinary: they were told that God's promise is true and that the Hour admits no doubt, and they replied that they had no idea what the Hour was. The Book simply places the two statements in sequence and lets the reader see the disproportion between them.

**"We Do Not Know What the Hour Is"**

The commentators give two readings of the clause. One takes it as a profession of uncertainty about whether the Hour is real at all; the other takes it as uncertainty about when it will arrive. Both readings are recorded in the major commentaries, and the second has a certain plausibility, since the deniers of Makkah repeatedly asked when the promise would be fulfilled. Yet the sentence does not stop at uncertainty. It continues into a statement of what the speakers do believe and what they refuse to accept, and that continuation gives away the fact that the profession of ignorance was not a plea for information. It was a way of dismissing a warning without having to answer it.

**Mockery as the Manner of the Answer**

The verse attaches a description to the way they spoke: they said it mockingly. Content and tone are both placed in the record, and the tone matters because it fixes the character of the reply. A person who genuinely wants to know what the Hour is will ask questions and wait for answers. A person who jeers has already settled the matter and is managing his audience. The sūrah has documented mockery as the practice of these men three times already, and the Book elsewhere states what happens to those who make a habit of it, saying that those who ridiculed the messengers were overtaken by the very thing they mocked (6:10 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”*; 21:41 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”*). The manner of the reply in this verse is the reason the answer at the judgment takes the form of a sentence rather than a discussion.
verses.33:
> And the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds will unfold before them, and they will be overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule

**What Was Hidden Becomes Visible**

The verb in the sentence describes something emerging into view. The sūrah's opponents had spent their lives treating the warnings as empty, and a person cannot sustain that treatment while the consequences of his conduct are visible to him. So the consequences were hidden, which is how the deniers were able to speak of promises and threats as poetry. The day described here ends that arrangement. The same phrasing appears in another chapter almost word for word, where the evil consequences of what people did unfold before them and they are overwhelmed by what they used to mock (39:48 — *“And the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds will unfold before them, and they will be overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule”*). The uniformity of the wording across the Book indicates that this is a fixed scene of judgment rather than a figure of speech, and the sūrah presents it as the ordinary result of a life being examined by its owner.

**Overwhelmed by What They Mocked**

The second half of the verse states the most exact justice in the chapter. What overwhelms the deniers is not an unrelated punishment imposed from outside; it is the very thing they laughed at, now arriving with full weight. The Book repeats this sentence in passage after passage, attaching it to the messengers who were ridiculed (6:10 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”*; 21:41 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”*), to nations that were destroyed (16:34 — *“Then the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds overtook them, and they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule”*), to a people whose respite ran out (11:8 — *“And if We delay their punishment until an appointed time, they will definitely say, “What is holding it back?” Indeed, on the Day it overtakes them, it will not be averted from them, and they will be overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule”*), and to whole communities who persisted in denying the signs (46:26 — *“But neither their hearing, sight, nor intellect were of any benefit to them whatsoever, since they persisted in denying Allah’s signs.”*). The repetition is deliberate. It establishes that the connection between mockery and ruin is not a coincidence of the judgment but a law that the Book has been announcing from the beginning. That the derision of the previous verse was not a harmless mood but the thing that would one day be handed back to its owner.

**No Injustice in the Accounting**

The Book never allows the punishment to be separated from the deeds, and it states the principle in a sentence that could serve as a heading for this whole scene: God does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves (10:44 — *“Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves”*). The verse before us follows the rule. The evil consequences that unfold belong to the people who produced them, the thing that overwhelms them is the object of their own derision, and the account is exact. Nothing has been added to the ledger by a judge who needed to be angry, and nothing has been forgotten by a court that wanted to be harsh. The suffering of the condemned is the working out of what they did, which is why the Book can describe a punishment this severe without describing it as cruelty.
verses.34:
> It will be said, “This Day We will neglect you as you neglected the meeting of this Day of yours! Your home will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers

**The Verdict Delivered as Speech**

The sentence begins with the passive report that it will be said, so that the emphasis falls on the words rather than on the speaker, though the following clause makes the speaker plain: the voice says we, and it is God who is not named. The judgment in the Book is often conducted in this manner, as a spoken address that the condemned hear and understand, rather than as a mechanical process operating on them from a distance. The condemned are told the meaning of what is happening to them while it happens. That detail preserves the chapter's picture of the judgment as a hearing with a verdict rather than a natural disaster. It also gives the sentence its force, since a punishment that arrives with an explanation cannot be dismissed as bad luck.

**Neglect Answered With Neglect**

The word translated against neglect is the ordinary verb for forgetting, and the Book's use of it for God is a deliberate mirroring: their treatment of the appointed day is returned to them in the same coin. The commentators explain by noting that the Book elsewhere makes God's forgetting mean abandonment rather than a lapse of knowledge, since nothing is outside his knowledge. The construction recurs in several chapters: those who took religion as amusement were told that God would ignore them as they ignored the meeting of that day (7:51 — *“˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs and for rejecting Our revelations.”*). The hypocrites forgot God and were forgotten in turn (9:67 — *“The hypocrites, both men and women, are all alike: they encourage what is evil, forbid what is good, and withhold ˹what is in˺ their hands. They neglected Allah, so He neglected them. Surely the hypocrites are the rebellious”*); a man who neglected the revelations is told that he is neglected that day (20:126 — *“Allah will respond, “It is so, just as Our revelations came to you and you neglected them, so Today you are neglected.”*); and the warned are told to taste the punishment for neglecting the meeting of their day, with the promise that God will neglect them too (32:14 — *“So taste ˹the punishment˺ for neglecting the meeting of this Day of yours. We ˹too˺ will certainly neglect you. And taste the torment of eternity for what you used to do”*). The measure is exact and the Book states it without softening.
verses.35:
> This is because you made a mockery of Allah’s revelations, and were deluded by ˹your˺ worldly life.” So ˹from˺ that Day ˹on˺ they will not be taken out of the Fire, nor will they be allowed to appease ˹their Lord˺

**The Reason Stated to Their Faces**

The Book never leaves a punishment unexplained. The sentence begins with a word of causation, and what follows is a short account of the two things that led to the verdict: mockery of the revelations, and the deception of worldly life. That pattern holds in the sūrah's other judgment scenes, where the accused are told precisely what they are being punished for. There is a purpose in the clarity. A verdict that cannot be understood could be resented as arbitrary, and the Book removes that possibility by naming the offence in ordinary words at the moment the sentence is passed. The condemned are not left to guess what they did wrong. They are told, in the second person, with the whole assembly listening.

**Mockery Named First**

The list puts the mockery of the revelations ahead of the delusion of the world, and the order reflects the sūrah's own account. The seventh verse pronounced woe on the sinful liar, the eighth described the man who hears and walks away, the ninth made derision a habit, the twenty-fourth recorded the mockers' arguments, and the thirty-second quoted their scoffing words at the judgment itself. The charge now gathers all of it into a single clause. What the men did with the message was not a private opinion but an activity: they took the revelations and turned them into material for jokes, in public, before audiences that they were trying to keep from believing. The Book treats that labour as the substance of their crime, and it names it first because everything else followed from it.

**Deluded by the Worldly Life**

The second cause is deception, and the Book uses it constantly for the relationship between a person and the present world. The world is said to have deluded the deniers (3:185 — *“Every soul will taste death. And you will only receive your full reward on the Day of Judgment. Whoever is spared from the Fire and is admitted into Paradise will ˹indeed˺ triumph, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”*), to be nothing more than play, amusement, luxury.

Competition (57:20 — *“Know that this worldly life is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children. This is like rain that causes plants to grow, to the delight of the planters. But later the plants dry up and you see them wither, then they are reduced to chaff. And in the Hereafter there will be either severe punishment or forgiveness and pleasure of Allah, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”*), to be a pleasure that distracts from what matters (9:38 — *“O believers! What is the matter with you that when you are asked to march forth in the cause of Allah, you cling firmly to ˹your˺ land? Do you prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter? The enjoyment of this worldly life is insignificant compared to that of the Hereafter”*), to be a fleeting enjoyment compared with the Hereafter (13:26 — *“But the life of this world, compared to the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment”*), and to be the home of settlement only for those who have understood what it is (40:39 — *“O my people! This worldly life is only ˹a fleeting˺ enjoyment, whereas the Hereafter is truly the home of settlement”*). None of these passages says that the created world is evil. The sūrah itself has just spent a dozen verses praising the sea, the rain, and the winds as gifts. The deception is not the world's existence but its promise: it presents itself as permanent and enough, and it cannot deliver on either.

**The Door That Stays Closed**

The sentence then closes the case with a firm statement: they will not be taken out of the Fire. The Book's accounts of the Hereafter do not include a second probation for those who reach this point, and it explains the reason through the plea of the condemned themselves. In one passage the wrongdoers beg to be sent back to do good rather than what they used to do, and the answer informs them that they were given lives long enough for anyone who wanted to take heed, and that the warner had already come (35:37 — *“We will do good, unlike what we used to do.”*). Another verse reports that if they were sent back they would only return to what they had been forbidden, and calls them liars (6:28 — *“Even if they were to be sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden. Indeed they are liars”*). The refusal is not a refusal of mercy in the abstract. It is a refusal to run an experiment that has already been tried.
verses.36:
> So all praise is for Allah—Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of all worlds

**Praise Placed After the Judgment**

The chapter has just finished a scene of condemnation, and the verse that follows it is a declaration of praise. The shift is not a change of subject. The Book's habit is to state its praise at the moments where the truth of its claims has become undeniable, and the reckoning is the greatest of those moments, since it settles every dispute the sūrah has been tracing and answers every mocker it has described. Praise at that point is not a religious formula inserted to fill a gap. It is the response that the completed account of God's rule calls for, and the Book gives it in advance so that the reader can join in before the scene arrives. Other chapters close in the same way, with praise pronounced at the end of a long argument rather than at its beginning.

**Three Titles and a Widening Horizon**

The verse names God as Lord of the heavens, Lord of the earth, and Lord of all worlds, and the three titles build outward in a deliberate order. The heavens come first, then the earth, and then everything that exists. The structure is not a list of separate domains but a single ownership stated in increasing scope, and the final title leaves nothing outside it. The Book uses the same expression for the same purpose elsewhere, saying that praise belongs to God in the heavens and the earth (30:18 — *“all praise is for Him in the heavens and the earth—as well as in the afternoon, and at noon”*). The effect is to make the praise universal by its content rather than only by the sentiment of the speaker. A reader who declares that God is Lord of all worlds has made a claim about reality, not expressed a feeling.

**Praise as Instruction, Not Only Devotion**

The sentence is given to the reader to say, and the Book uses this construction frequently: a declaration of praise that doubles as a command to praise. The most famous occurrence is the opening of the Fātiḥah, where the words all praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds (1:2 — *“All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds”*) stand at the head of the recited book and are repeated in every prayer.

The same sentence recurs throughout the Qur'an, in the speech of the angels around the throne (39:75 — *“You will see the angels all around the Throne, glorifying the praises of their Lord, for judgment will have been passed on all with fairness.”*), in the greeting of the blessed in the Garden (10:10 — *“in which their prayer will be, “Glory be to You, O Allah!” and their greeting will be, “Peace!” and their closing prayer will be, “All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds!”*), among the saints who praise God for removing their sorrow (35:34 — *“And they will say, “Praise be to Allah, Who has kept away from us all ˹causes of˺ sorrow. Our Lord is indeed All-Forgiving, Most Appreciative”*), and in the invitation to call on God with sincere devotion (40:65 — *“He is the Ever-Living. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. So call upon Him with sincere devotion, ˹saying,˺ “All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.”*). A formula repeated this often is not decoration. It is the sentence the Book teaches its readers to say about the world.

**The Praise of Everything That Exists**

Other passages make the point that praise is not confined to human beings or to believers. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God (59:24 — *“Whatever is in the heavens and the earth ˹constantly˺ glorifies Him.”*), a statement that places the reader's own act of praise inside a chorus far larger than the assembly of his fellow believers. The sūrah has treated the created order as a book of signs since its opening verses, and this verse supplies the response that the signs were pointing toward. A person who has understood the argument of the chapter is not being asked to invent a sentiment; he is being placed alongside the creation in a declaration that everything belongs to the one who made it. Praise in that setting is closer to an acknowledgment of the facts than to a mood.
verses.37:
> To Him belongs ˹all˺ Majesty in the heavens and the earth. And He is the Almighty, All-Wise

**Majesty as a Property of Ownership**

The word rendered Majesty names greatness and the grandeur of a sovereign, and the verse places it in the same two realms it has been discussing since its third verse. The heavens and the earth hold no grandeur that does not belong to their owner; the phrase does not mean that his greatness is distributed across creation, but that everything in both realms acknowledges a greatness that is his alone. The Book uses the same construction at the close of other chapters, where it places the attributes of God after a survey of his rule, and the effect is always to leave the reader with a claim about God rather than a task to perform. The chapter has just pronounced praise; this verse states the ground on which praise rests.

**Where Else the Book Uses This Pair**

The pairing of Almighty and All-Wise recurs at the close of other sūrahs and always in the context of God's ownership and rule. One chapter lists it in a passage that ends with the glorification of everything in the heavens and the earth (59:24 — *“And He is the Almighty, All-Wise”*), and another uses it in a description of the knower of the seen and the unseen (64:18 — *“˹He is the˺ Knower of the seen and unseen—the Almighty, All-Wise”*). The formula also appears at the head of the chapters that open with ḥāʾ and mīm, as this sūrah has shown. The sūrah's final sentence is therefore not a private ending. It places the chapter inside a wider pattern of praise that the Book establishes elsewhere, and it lets the reader hear the last words of al-Jāthiyah as a line in a chorus rather than an isolated conclusion.
